title: Qin Great Wall
summary: After unifying China in 221 BCE, the Qin sent general Meng Tian north with 300,000 troops; he drove back the Xiongnu and joined older Qin, Zhao and Yan walls into a line the Shiji says ran over 10,000 li.
card: Once Qin had conquered its rivals in 221 BCE, the First Emperor turned to the northern frontier. His general Meng Tian pushed the Xiongnu out of the lands south of the Yellow River bend, and soldiers, convicts and resettled families linked the separate northern walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan into one line from Lintao to Liaodong. Sima Qian, who later travelled the line, judged that it was built with little regard for the people's strength.
what:
The Qin Great Wall is the first attempt to join China's separate northern walls into a single frontier. Its main written source is the Shiji of the Han historian Sima Qian. In the biography of Meng Tian, once Qin had swallowed the other states, the First Emperor (Qin Shi Huang) sent Meng Tian north with 300,000 men to drive out the Rong and Di peoples and take the lands south of the Yellow River, then built a long wall that followed the terrain and used natural strongholds from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east, more than 10,000 li in all. Meng Tian's army stayed in the field for more than ten years, based in Shang commandery, and his reputation, the text says, overawed the Xiongnu.

The basic annals of the First Emperor give tighter dates. In the emperor's 32nd year (215 BCE) Meng Tian led 300,000 troops against the Hu and took the Henan lands; in the 33rd year (214 BCE) the Xiongnu were driven back, 34 new counties were set up along the river from Yuzhong toward the Yin Mountains, and walls were built on the river as a frontier; in the 34th year (213 BCE) officials judged to have administered justice unfairly were banished to build the long wall. In the 36th year (211 BCE) 30,000 households were moved to the northern river lands and Yuzhong. The two chapters disagree on when the northern campaign began, either soon after unification in 221 BCE or in 215 BCE.

Modern heritage bodies describe the work as linking and restoring walls that the states of Qin, Zhao and Yan had built in the 3rd century BCE, extended west along the Yellow River toward Lanzhou and finished shortly before the Han took power. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, a forged order in his name forced Meng Tian to take poison. China's 2012 survey counts 3,680.26 km of surviving Qin and Han walls together, without separating the two dynasties.

uncertainty.note: Start: Shiji 88 places Meng Tian's northern command after the unification of 221 BCE and says his army was in the field more than ten years; Shiji 6 dates the northern offensive to the First Emperor's 32nd year (215 BCE) and wall-building to 214–213 BCE. End: Meng Tian's death in 210 BCE; ICOMOS says the system was completed shortly before the Han (206 BCE).

how: The Qin did not build a new wall from nothing. ICOMOS describes the work as restoring and linking walls that Qin, Zhao and Yan had already built in the 3rd century BCE, and SACH's survey report likewise says the northern walls of the three states were connected. The sequence in the Shiji is military first: Meng Tian's army drove the Hu out of the Henan lands (215 BCE), Qin then founded new counties along the Yellow River and fortified the river itself as a frontier (214 BCE), crossed the river to hold Gaoque, Yangshan and Beijia, and built forts and watch posts to keep the Rong out. The wall itself followed the lie of the land, using cliffs, ridges and passes as part of the barrier. Labour combined the army, convicts and officials banished for unjust judgments, while the frontier was filled with exiles and, in 211 BCE, 30,000 resettled households. Surviving Qin and Han walls are mostly earth and stone. In 212 BCE the Straight Road was cut from Jiuyuan to Yunyang to move troops north. How many workers died is not recorded in any source opened for this record.
why_it_matters: This was the moment separate state walls became an imperial frontier. By joining the Qin, Zhao and Yan walls and fortifying the new river counties, Qin drew a line between the farming empire and the steppe that later dynasties, above all the Han, extended and rebuilt. In the short term it pushed the Xiongnu back: the Han writer Jia Yi, quoted by Sima Qian, claimed the Hu were driven more than 700 li away and no longer dared to graze their horses to the south. It also moved people: convicts, banished officials and 30,000 households were sent to the frontier. Its cost became part of the case against Qin. Sima Qian, writing under the Han, said Meng Tian had treated the people's strength lightly when the empire was newly united and its wounds unhealed, and he rejected Meng Tian's own deathbed claim that his only crime was cutting the veins of the earth. Had Qin not taken and walled the Henan lands, the Xiongnu would have kept pastures within easy reach of the Qin heartland, and the early Han, which faced a powerful Xiongnu confederation, would have inherited a weaker northern frontier.

perspectives.holder: Shiji chapter 88 (biography of Meng Tian); ICOMOS (1987) and UNESCO date the work from about 220 BCE
perspectives.account: Meng Tian was sent north as soon as Qin had unified the realm in 221 BCE, and his army remained in the field for more than ten years.

perspectives.holder: Shiji chapter 6 (basic annals of the First Emperor)
perspectives.account: The northern offensive came in the emperor's 32nd year (215 BCE), prompted by a text presented to him saying that Qin would be destroyed by the Hu; walls and counties followed in 214–213 BCE.

perspectives.holder: Sima Qian, closing judgement of Shiji chapter 88
perspectives.account: Having seen the walls and posts himself, he held that Meng Tian squandered the people's strength when he should have urged the emperor to relieve a war-weary population, so his execution was deserved and had nothing to do with harming the earth's veins.

perspectives.holder: Jia Yi, essay on the faults of Qin, quoted at the end of Shiji chapter 6
perspectives.account: The wall served as the empire's hedge: it pushed the Xiongnu back more than 700 li and stopped them grazing their horses to the south.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the start date (221 vs 215 BCE in the two Shiji chapters), of the route between Lintao and Liaodong (not separable from Han walls in the survey, and Lintao's location is not pinned), and the death toll, which no opened source quantifies.
parent_reconciliation: The hub's 21,196.18 km all-period total includes 3,680.26 km of surviving Qin and Han walls together; the Shiji's 'more than 10,000 li' is a Qin-era claim in Qin units and is not comparable with the survey figure.
